articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6: Extended Look Sparks Netflix Viewership Spike, as Streamer Experiences Momentary Wobble
articles.summary: Netflix US viewership spiked by 50% yesterday as Rockstar debuted its Grand Theft Auto 6: Extended Look.
articles.body:
Netflix US viewership spiked by 50% yesterday as Rockstar debuted its Grand Theft Auto 6: Extended Look.

That's according to audience data provided to IGN by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower , when comparing Netflix's US audience to the same time on the previous day.

Compared to the streamer's average US viewership over the past 12 weeks on a Thursday, mobile use was up almost 50%. Web visitors soared by 125%, meanwhile, as countless subscribers tuned in from their PCs (perhaps sneakily watching from work or classes).

While the launch of Netflix's GTA 6 broadcast was ultimately successful, users in multiple countries reported experiencing momentary technical difficulties at the moment of its premiere. If you saw the below error screen — featuring someone's hand and a very wonky cake — you certainly were not alone. Countless users reported seeing similar across social media, including high-profile streamers, and we certainly saw the same here at IGN. Thankfully, the problem resolved itself within around 30 seconds.

"Utilizing lexicon-stirring events tied to notable IP has helped expand Netflix's appeal as an all-encompassing entertainment platform," Abe Yousef, Senior Insights Analyst said. "By aligning itself with the launch of a highly anticipated console title, Netflix is converting heightened consumer interest into re-engagement from lapsed viewers and sign-ups from non-subscribers."

Sensor Tower data has also given an update on GTA 6's pre-order numbers, with more than 4.5 million copies already sold, generating nearly $450 million in revenue — and that's before the GTA 6: Extended Look aired. (It seems likely that number has now risen significantly higher.) Of the copies sold so far, more than three quarters are on PlayStation 5.

90% of pre-orders are for the game's $100 Ultimate Edition, meanwhile. This is an impressive statistic, though this will likely skew higher than at launch due to pre-order customers typically being more hardcore players.

IGN is one of the very few outlets to have been given an exclusive preview of GTA 6 . We also have details on GTA 6's romance system , how long GTA 6 will take to beat , every GTA 6 side activity we've spotted so far , and how GTA 6's bigger map compares to past Rockstar games as part of our exhaustive and ongoing coverage. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto III – The Legacy Review - IGN
articles.summary:
Grand Theft Auto III legacy review by Luke Reilly. Reviewed on PlayStation 2. 
"Grand Theft Auto III, in its original form, is a frustrating and regularly cumbersome game to play in 2026. Its unforgiving need to manually return to mission markers and start from scratch encourages a very careful and conservative sort of playstyle that clashes with the chaotic level of freedom its world and systems otherwise encourage. On top of this, its shooting is admittedly fussy and frustrating, and its cast of shallow and simplistic characters are amongst the least memorable of the series. Within that initial salvo of 3D GTA games, Vice City oozed dramatically more style and swagger, and San Andreas offered astonishingly increased size and scope. It didn’t just change the trajectory of the GTA series forever – it changed the business. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto III – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: Replaying the pioneering 2001 classic 25 years later and paying tribute to the game that didn’t just change the trajectory of the GTA series forever – it changed the business.
articles.body:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today, we go back to the game that changed this series forever: Grand Theft Auto III.

Playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2026 is a little like watching a home movie of Usain Bolt learning to walk. It’s a little wobbly, and it hasn’t quite got the whole process worked out yet, but through a modern lens it comes with a fascinating awareness you’re seeing the first steps of a field-defining juggernaut. In the late ’90s, GTA games had found success showing us the unique brand of freedom they offered within their sandbox-style cities – but the old school, top-down approach was a dated aesthetic in contrast to the fully 3D worlds that were first beginning to emerge during this era. In 2001, GTA III arrived as a completely different proposition, instantly reinventing the series as the new cutting edge of open-world action games.

It’s true that its already annoying targeting system is doubly frustrating by modern standards, and its time-consuming mission restarts do feel particularly punitive 25 years on. However, I’ve found it impossible not to admire how well it otherwise weaves together its driving, action, story, and exploration within a dynamic 3D world, considering it accomplished this before there was any sort of proper blueprint for doing so. Sure, GTA III didn’t get everything right immediately – but you’ve got to walk before you can run.

Playing GTA III in such close proximity to GTA 2, I’m actually quickly reminded of how immediately the former feels like the game that was actually teased by the latter’s eye-catching, live-action intro. The gritty, New York-based short promotional film Rockstar produced for GTA 2 (and subsequently trimmed down to serve as its intro) never felt remotely connected to the quasi-cyberpunk setting of that game – but it feels perfectly aligned to GTA III. The fact that GTA III made good on a cheque that GTA 2 bounced made it all the more special upon its arrival. GTA 2 only left me desperately wanting a game in the spirit of what I saw in that promo film. Two years later, GTA III delivered it.

GTA III kept a couple of noticeable elements established by its predecessor – like its hilarious array of custom radio commercials, its random fascination with Elvis Presley, and even an optional top-down camera – but it completely discarded its divisive time period, indeterminable location, and retro-futuristic fleet of vehicles. Instead, it opted for something credible, contemporary, and recognisable, and returned to the original GTA’s New York homage: Liberty City.

While GTA III’s voice cast is a murderers’ row of iconic Hollywood crime fiction actors – including Frank Vincent, Michael Madsen, Joe Pantoliano, Robert Loggia, Michael Rapaport, Kyle MacLachlan, and Debi Mazar – none gallops away as the star of the game. In fact, with a silent protagonist and an otherwise very simple story propped up by a supporting crew of broad and largely one-dimensional criminal stereotypes, it’s Liberty City itself that perhaps emerges as GTA III’s greatest character.

Liberty City is split into three distinct boroughs that are rationed out as the story unfolds. We begin in Portland, an area defined by its grimy industrial sector and seedy red light district, before scampering to the Manhattan-inspired Staunton Island when the situation turns sour. Staunton Island is a wholly different backdrop; it’s highly commercial and features towering skyscrapers and a lush and centrally located park. The third area is Shoreside Vale, which is a leafy, suburban zone that’s otherwise dominated by a large airport and dam. Unfortunately, Shoreside Vale is actually the least interesting of the three boroughs, lacking both the personality of Portland and the density of Staunton Island. I’ll give it a nod for being the home of the infamously tricky to fly Dodo, but it’s otherwise a bit of a disappointing shift.

The dimensions of Liberty City are extremely modest compared to its later reinvention in GTA IV – and it’s absolutely dwarfed by modern open-world standards – but that was of no consequence back in 2001. At that time, it was unlike any game world we’d ever visited – and its nature as a place where day became night and clear weather turned to rain made it somewhere that felt alive in a fundamentally new way. Stand still in GTA III’s Liberty City and life will simply go on around you. Traffic flows, pedestrians pass, and the Earth spins. None of this would be particularly impressive today, but it was back then. The feeling I got re-immersing myself in GTA III and being transported back to that moment in my life has been a potent one.

The template DMA Design established for the top-down GTA games unsurprisingly remained in place for GTA III. That is, whether you’re behind the wheel or on foot, everything happens in the same space. There are no “driving” levels or “action” levels. There are no levels at all. There’s one map, and player agency is the number one priority. Yes, there are many instances where the missions may compel you to use a particular vehicle but, for the most part, you’re in complete control of how you move around the world. Grab whatever car you want, and head in any direction you choose.

25 years on, the novelty of this freedom has somewhat expired – but in 2001 it was really nothing short of revolutionary. The powerful might of the PlayStation 2 had given GTA III the ability to push far beyond what was possible on the original PlayStation, transforming its top-down chaos into something modern, immediate, dangerous, and cinematic. Very simply, you were now in the world – not floating above it. It no longer felt like playing cops and robbers with toy cars – it felt like holidaying in a Michael Mann action sequence.

GTA III’s driving physics are a little slippier and floatier than they are in the more modern installments of the series, but they’re still quite easy to come to terms with in 2026. They don’t quite have the weight and inertia needed to be able to consistently flick them into extravagant J-turns and the like, but they feel otherwise adequate. There are many open-world action/driving games released over the last 25 years that I’ve found twitchier, sloppier, or more superficial than GTA III, that much I can assure you. At any rate, being behind the wheel is also the only way to hear all the wacky radio commercials, which once again had me grinning – or the cavalcade of insane callers on Chatterbox FM.

What has aged quite horribly, however, is the third-person shooting – which was arguably already the weakest pillar of GTA III back in 2001 (at least on PS2, which didn’t have the benefit of the 2002 PC version’s mouse functionality). The main issue is that not all of the weapons support free aim. Only the M16-style assault rifle, rocket launcher, and sniper rifle can be manually aimed; everything else must rely on the auto-lock targeting system. This doesn’t sound like a huge sacrifice, until you find yourself in a significant firefight on the streets of Liberty City, and you end up inadvertently cycling your reticule onto nearby grandmas, allies, or overzealous paramedics because the system doesn’t prioritise the armed assailants blasting at you.

The complete lack of mission checkpoints wouldn’t really pass muster today, either. It certainly reduces the amount of chaos I’m willing to get into, considering it’s a more efficient use of time to try to pick off enemies from as far away as possible and lean on any cheesy strategy that works. The need to continuously drive all the way back to mission start bubbles after failing an objective was already a pretty aggravating chore in 2001, but it was softened by the fact I was just a university student living at home, with a part-time job and oodles of free time. In 2026, I’m all out of oodles.

Despite generating widespread controversy (and, quite possibly, thanks to it) GTA III was monumentally successful, greatly exceeding sales expectations. It ultimately sold more than 14.5 million copies, 11.6 million of which were on PS2 – where it would become the fifth highest-selling game on the system. However, while its commercial impact is one thing, its cultural impact is something else altogether.

Perhaps the easiest way to understand the immense legacy of GTA III is to look at everything that came after it. That is, everything that ultimately paraphrased the modern open-world philosophy that GTA III essentially established – a large, explorable environment with missions distributed throughout it, optional side activities, a varied fleet of vehicles, endless NPCs, believable radio stations and music, and the freedom to poke the world and see how hard it pokes back. Yes, GTA III owes its own reverence to the projects that inspired it in the first place, with Rockstar’s Sam Houser memorably explaining it as Zelda meets Goodfellas at the time, but there is no denying the influence of the template it established. True Crime, Saints Row, Watch Dogs, Sleeping Dogs; each of them borrowed or riffed on concepts GTA III created.

It’s hard to say what the open-world action/driving genre looks like were it not for GTA III. Does it still evolve at all? Absolutely. As I discussed in our GTA 2 Legacy Review , the dawn of 3D driving games was already upon us at that time – and several had already begun to blend third-person action into them. The genre was already here, albeit in its infancy. Driver 3 was always going to be an evolution of the ambitious Driver 2. Mafia had been in development since late 1998. The Getaway had been in development for the original PlayStation before becoming a PS2 project. We certainly can’t pretend things weren’t happening in this space.

However, we also can’t pretend that any of these early examples accomplished what GTA III did with nearly the same aplomb. We can’t pretend they contained the same unhinged energy, or the same innovative blend of driving, action, story, and exploration. There, GTA III stands alone. Its immense success didn’t happen by accident; it happened because it uncovered and established a formula that gamers found irresistible – and the series has been the yardstick for the genre for 25 years because of it.

Grand Theft Auto III, in its original form, is a frustrating and regularly cumbersome game to play in 2026. Its unforgiving need to manually return to mission markers and start from scratch encourages a very careful and conservative sort of playstyle that clashes with the chaotic level of freedom its world and systems otherwise encourage. On top of this, its shooting is admittedly fussy and frustrating, and its cast of shallow and simplistic characters are amongst the least memorable of the series. Within that initial salvo of 3D GTA games, Vice City oozed dramatically more style and swagger, and San Andreas offered astonishingly increased size and scope. However, neither of these legendary games can lay claim to being GTA III – just improved versions of it.

It occupies a unique place in the series' storied history. While it didn’t pioneer every part of the modern formula for open-world games, it brought driving, action, story, and exploration together in a radically new way. It didn’t just change the trajectory of the GTA series forever – it changed the business. There are few games that can claim to be as innovative as GTA III, and fewer still as permanently trendsetting. GTA III didn’t just show us what an open world game was. It showed us what an open world game could be.

For more reflections on the incredible Grand Theft Auto series, you can read our new Legacy Reviews of Grand Theft Auto and Grand Theft Auto 2 , with more to follow over the coming months.

articles.title: Gallipoli Review: Beautiful, Brutal, and Fun
articles.summary: Gallipoli is the most beautiful game in the WW1 series yet, with excellent maps, fun new classes, and a continued focus on teamwork in order to win.
articles.body:
Well lads, we've done it. We've landed ashore and now it's time to rush forward into enemy territory for God and King. The rules of engagement are simple: there's only one rule, and that rule… is to have fun. And maybe make some friends along the way? BlackMill Games' Gallipoli, the fourth in its well-established WW1 series, is its best-looking and strongest WW1 project to date, and I'm ready to party like it's 1915. Not only is Gallipoli a step above its predecessors in terms of its graphics and gameplay, it does an exemplary job of conveying a sense of historical accuracy while remaining fun to play. So chaps, keep a stiff upper lip and let's charge into certain doom, shall we?

Gallipoli is set in the Middle Eastern front, the only World War 1 front not yet featured in one of BlackMill's games. For some historical context, the forces here are primarily the Ottoman Empire versus the British Empire, a lumbering old empire in its failing days versus an empire that was still the most powerful in the world. If you, like me, grew up in the good old US of A, you probably spent zero time in school learning anything about the Middle Eastern Front of World War 1, because America didn't do anything in that part of the world during that part of the first World War. In contrast, in Australia and New Zealand, the national day of remembrance established to acknowledge the tragedy of the Gallipoli campaign has completely usurped Remembrance Day in terms of national significance.

Since World War 1 is maybe the most impactful event in the history of humankind, it's a shame vast parts of it often go undiscussed. This is something that makes Gallipoli all the more appealing to me. I want to learn more about this part of history now. I would venture to say I'm a little more well-versed than most in World War 1 history, but I've only ever really studied the Western Front and its long lines of muddy, rat-infested trenches.

When I'm playing Gallipoli and I start into a map, like Anzac Cove (which also happens to be my favorite), I find myself compelled to learn more. The loading screens have brief snippets of historical context to read, which is great, although it's not enough to scratch the itch I have. It's just a beautiful outgrowth of an excellent game; to be such a compelling experience as a video game as to make me want to learn more about the actual history.

If you're on the attacking side of the Anzac Cove map – that is, the British Empire – you start the match being rowed to shore in double-ender rowboats. We've all seen the scenes, both real and created by Hollywood, featuring the storming of Normandy during the Second World War. Anzac Cove is almost the same, but there are no diesel-powered landing craft opening their ramps into a hail of enemy bullets. Just Commonwealth troops scrambling out of painfully slow, wildly exposed wooden boats under a torrent of machine gun fire.

The uniforms at the start of World War 1 were basically just fancy clothes for army men; nothing like the armor and helmets of today. I love that Gallipoli captures the schism between the rapid advancement of warfighting technology and the lag that followed while armies had to figure out, in real time, how to fight this new and horrible type of war. Men were thrusting themselves into meat grinders, and the answer to the high casualty rates was simply "throw more men in." It's an era where the technology of war had fast outpaced the strategies to fight it.

For example, the machine gun. Gallipoli has two machine gunner classes: light, and the new heavy machine gunner class. While they have different abilities and missions, their ultimate goal is to spit out as much lead as is possible in the shortest amount of time. This will either provide cover for advancing troops or, in what I find to be one of the coolest additions to Gallipoli, terrify your opponents. In Gallipoli, you now get experience points for laying down suppressive fire, but that fire also has an effect on players.

During one match I found myself pinned down and separated from my squad, and the enemy team was laying down a constant barrage of fire in my direction. Suddenly, the terror of it all got to my character and I went into a panic mode. My vision was blurred. I couldn't maintain a steady aim down the sights of my rifle. In essence, I had lost my nerve, and that element of the gameplay ultimately caused me to take the L and have to respawn.

What a fantastic way to add another layer of realism. Does it suck when bullets are whizzing over your head and suddenly you lose your faculties? Yes, of course it does. But that's just an extra dimension to the experience, and one that I didn't think I'd appreciate as much as I do. And it goes both ways, too. You can panic oncoming troops and, while machine gunners have it easier by means of bullet volume, I was able to panic my enemies just by firing at them with my standard-issue rifle. On top of another wrinkle of realism, it also means shots that don't land on their intended targets can still provide a benefit to you and your team.

The machine gun wasn't entirely new by the time WW1 kicked off, but there hadn't been a test of it at scale to that point. At the start of the war, people basically had no idea how to approach them on the battlefield. Thanks to the suppression and panic systems, that feeling is replicated well here in Gallipoli. The heavy machine gunner is tasked with building machine guns wherever they can be built but, strategically speaking, you want to build them where they can help hold a line – or help advance your troops. It's so wonderful when you're laying down fire and suppressing the enemy and your team is able to break through and advance.

While the heavy machine gunner builds machine gun embankments, the light machine gunner brings his along for the ride. This is another thing I really like about Gallipoli; you can't John-Rambo your way through a map hip firing a light machine gun. That's Hollywood stuff. Unlike Call of Duty, or most modern first-person shooters, guns in Gallipoli behave like they would in real life. That means trying to hip fire your light machine gun is pointless. The barrel swings wildly and the shots are so scattered it doesn't even panic your opponents. In fact, it makes you a nice target instead. If you want to do well with the light machine gun, you’d better put your face in the dirt and lay down some covering fire for the fellas to make that final push.

Realism with guns and weapons is part of the experience. Rifles and pistols lose their effectiveness depending on range. Not all bullets are built equally, and a rifle that does well at mid or close range is basically useless at long range. Even if you do hit a target from across the field, depending on the gun, it might not stop them or even do much damage. Pistols, the weapons of the officer class, are a great example of this. With their short barrels and powerful kick, hitting a target at any sort of distance is a challenge both in the real world and in Gallipoli. If you're coming into this expecting the kind of gunplay in CoD or Battlefield, you're going to be pretty bummed out. I'm not disparaging those franchises, either (I love CoD multiplayer and review it every year for IGN), but Gallipoli is focused on realism more than dynamic, clippable action.

And yet, the action is still present. It's chaotic and brutal and confusing, and I'm loving it. One really awesome new addition is how dust can change everything about a battle. When an artillery barrage or a mortar strike happens, it kicks up a hauntingly beautiful cloud of dust that obscures everything. Suddenly you can't see your target or your goal. It works to both obscure the enemy and to provide cover for yourself, but it remains mostly a hindrance to troop movement.

More than once, I almost fired on a teammate who emerged from a dust cloud seemingly out of nowhere. The same is true in the trenches. I found myself running into a player and almost shooting (or stabbing them) multiple times. In a game like CoD, I find this frustrating. In Gallipoli, however, it's all part of the fog of war.

Yes, you will get dinged for harming teammates – and there is no option to turn off team killing. It's entirely possible to call in an artillery barrage as the officer class and have it rain down on the heads of your own team. Thankfully,I haven't had that experience, because I'm a thoughtful officer who's concerned about the welfare of my boys and wants to see them make it home. But I've definitely accidentally bayoneted one or two of my teammates in the trenches when things were getting a little too crazy. Sorry about that.

Aside from the dust and the risk of wiping out large swaths of your team with artillery strikes and other off-map support, like aircraft runs, when you do manage to catch the other team bunched up and the points start piling up, it's just wonderful. I was able to successfully take out large numbers of the approaching British not once, but several times while they held tenuously to their position on the V Beach map. It was as exhilarating as I'm sure it was horribly frustrating for the other team.

There are four new classes in Gallipoli: stretcher bearer, heavy machine gunner (which I already talked about), ammo bearer, and the bomber. Stretcher bearer is the medic class, and I found that I was extremely effective in helping my team reach our objectives by building med stations as we advanced, and keeping my head down to heal and revive my squadmates.

Healing and reviving is particularly effective in trench warfare, but there's still plenty of opportunity to shoot the enemy, too. Ammo bearer also has a support role, refreshing squad mates with ammo by either dropping ammo boxes – or straight up just handing them a fresh mag. The bomber is exactly what it sounds like: a soldier armed with grenades and homemade explosive devices made with metal food tins. Fun fact, the metal tin "brands" are all fictional creations by BlackMill Games, and there seems to be an almost endless supply of different ones to hurl.

Of the new classes, I like heavy machine gunner and stretcher bearer the best. The bomber is a little difficult for me to really get into because I don't feel like it's as effective when defending as it is when attacking. Even then, landing a grenade or bomb where it can do the most damage honestly takes a little bit of luck. It's not so much there's an RNG element or anything, but you need to be able to know where the enemy is to get a successful lob – and the problem with war is that if you can see the enemy, the enemy can see you. That being said, when I was able to toss a grenade into a crater filled with prone enemies, holy cow did THAT rule.

Of all the classes available, the returning sniper class is probably the most fun to play, at least for me. I was able to post up and find a pinch point more than once, where the enemies just kept feeding themselves right into the sights of my scope. It's so satisfying, and the best thing about it is there's only one sniper allowed per team. In fact, other than rifleman and engineers, all the classes have caps on how many are allowed in a match, which prevents the entire team from just running around using sniper rifles like normal weapons, like in CoD. There's no quick scoping here, thankfully.

Perhaps the greatest part of Gallipoli, however, is the player base. You may have noticed that this review is coming after the game's release. That's because I wanted to make sure I got in some hours playing with real people. By and large, those real people delivered the goods. This is one of those kinds of games that attracts a certain kind of unc; that is, people like me – and almost everyone in every match is there to play Gallipoli as it was designed to be played.

You cannot successfully win if everyone is running around like it's a death match. One of the least appealing parts of Call of Duty multiplayer to me each year are the objective-based matches. No one does any of the objective stuff; they just run around working on their K/D ratio. Not in Gallipoli. Almost everyone is doing what needs to be done.

And better still, it's not intimidating. Yes, you're going to get those people in the chat chastizing the team for not doing everything to their liking, but otherwise you can just jump into a game, stay with your squad, and have a great time. It's not like CS:GO, where my one experience trying a ranked match ended three minutes in after being ruthlessly berated by my team before being kicked out.

People are pretty chill here, and they want more people to play the game – because the more people play it, the more fun it is. When everyone locks in, listens to one another, sticks to their role, and makes smart decisions, Gallipoli is a sublime experience. It's one of the best multiplayer shooters I can think of in terms of squad-based, objective-focused gameplay. It just flows so wonderfully as a game, while also doing an incredible job of recreating the hellish nightmare that was World War 1 warfare.

Seth Macy is Senior Social Commerce Producer, and just wants to be your friend. You can find him on social media sites @SethFromMaine.

articles.title: DLSS 5 leaked and modders are putting Nvidia’s AI effects on everything
articles.summary: Modders are applying an unofficial version of Nvidia’s DLSS 5 to a bunch of different games after code for the AI upscaling tech appeared in an early-access build of NBA 2K27.
articles.body: Modders are trying out an unofficial version of Nvidia’s DLSS 5 on Skyrim, Cyberpunk 2077, GTA V, and a bunch of other games after code for the AI upscaling tech appeared in an early-access build of NBA 2K27. Members of the RenoDX modding channel on Discord reportedly found a way to extract the DLSS “Neural Rendering” file and apply it to Control before it expanded to other games, as reported earlier by Notebook Check and VideoCardz. In one video, a person shows how Control protagonist Jesse Faden’s facial features become more and less defined as they tweak various DLSS 5 settings enabled by the RenoDX modders. With the “Neural Uplift” setting disabled within the mod, Jesse’s face has a smooth, uniform look. But as soon as the modder turns this feature on with one of the presets, her face becomes paler, with more visible laugh lines and what looks like more makeup smudged beneath her eyes. [Media: Another modder appears to have gotten the DLSS 5 tech working in GTA: San Andreas, where it seems to apply a filter effect to CJ’s face and enhances textures across the city. It also makes shadows on CJ’s face and his surrounding environment more pronounced, while the city’s lighting changes from a warm to a cool tone as the modder adjusts one of the sliders. Several other videos are floating around the web as well, with the DLSS 5 mod bringing more definition to the cartoony look of a Palworld character and altering the intensity of shadows. There are countless other videos floating around on the web (with more likely to come). [Image: [Image: The DLSS 5 mod changes the lighting in GTA: San Andreas and makes CJ’s face look more defined. | Image: Jessica Natalia Mods via YouTube The modders trying out the mod say that it impacts game performance. One person trying out the mod with Final Fantasy VII Rebirth says it “halves” their frames per second (FPS) and that “swapping between presets eats a TON of vram.” You can see the frames drop from 90 to 29 FPS as another modder adjusts the sliders in GTA V. Modders had the unofficial version of DLSS 5 running on RTX 50-series chips, but now some have gotten it working on RTX 4090 and RTX 4080 chips, too, according to VideoCardz. Much like the reveal of DLSS 5, reactions to the unofficial version of the tech are mixed. While some players think the filters improve the appearance of games, others call them AI slop and say they look too much like an “AI-enhanced” filter you’d apply to images. [Media: Nvidia first announced DLSS 5 in March, which uses AI to bring “photoreal lighting and materials” to game graphics in real-time. Demos showing DLSS 5 across Resident Evil Requiem, Starfield, and Hogwarts Legacy sparked immediate backlash, with many players complaining about characters’ “yassified” or generic looks. Others raised concerns that it could alter a developer’s vision for their characters, to which Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang responded by saying the tool “doesn’t change the artistic control.” DLSS 5 is set to officially launch this fall.

articles.title: EA Motive's Iron Man Game Trailer Seemingly Leaked With Early Look at Gameplay
articles.summary: Gameplay footage from what appears to be EA Motive Studio's Iron Man game has leaked online.
articles.body:
Gameplay footage from what appears to be EA Motive Studio's Iron Man game has leaked online.

Video for what seems to be EA's long-in-development Iron Man game started circulating on social media today. It's a bit more than a few cobbled-together clips, too, showing a (very unfinished) project that features not only Tony Stark's Iron Man, but what seem to be a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier and potentially other characters that Marvel fans may recognize.

The footage, which appeaers to be part of a trailer from an early-in-development build, looks like the kind of thing you'd expect from an Iron Man game. Tony can be seen flying under bridges and through city streets, beating up armored bad guys in between shots of him tinkering on new suit technology, giving the impression that EA Motive is crafting something that will have players traveling around the world.

The allegedly leaked footage for the Iron Man game promises that players will be shooting missiles, using arm-mounted lasers, and throwing missiles at tanks. We won't share any of that here, but if the footage does turn out to be real, it would seem rumors that Motive's Iron Man game was canceled have been greatly exaggerated.

Interestingly, this isn't even the first time this week footage for an unfinished Iron Man game found its way on the net. Monday, video for what seemed to be Avalanche Studios' Iron Man game also surfaced online . It's a different project that was rumored to be in development in the early 2010s before its eventual cancellation. While that team's vision will never see the light of day, nothing is suggesting EA's Iron Man will meet the same fate.

Motive officially revealed its take on the character almost exactly four years ago in 2022. Despite the immense amount of hype the Dead Space remake and Star Wars: Squadrons developer managed to generate at the time, things have been distressingly quiet since.

Our last real update arrived in April 2024, when the team reassured fans that its Iron Man game remained an "important priority" as EA brought it in to work on Battlefield 6. With little else besides a teaser image to keep fans occupied, some had started to worry the team's Marvel project may have kicked the can. However, for now, the game is still officially considered to very much be in development.

Marvel's Wolverine Screenshots (August 2026)

"In parallel, development continues to move forward on our Iron Man project, led by Olivier Proulx (Executive Producer) and Ian Frazier (Creative Director)," Motive general manager Patrick Klaus said in 2024. "The team made excellent progress this year, hitting a major internal milestone and laying a robust foundation for the journey ahead. Iron Man is an important priority for Motive, and I’m very proud of the work we’ve accomplished so far."

While it's unclear when footage from today's supposed leak would have been captured, it suggests Motive has been steadily moving along behind the scenes. In an environment where fans clamor for Spider-Man and Wolverine video games, an Iron Man game could (hopefully) have a lot of potential. EA had no comment to share when contacted by IGN.

While we wait for updates as Motive hammers away at its Iron Man game, you can check out the Tony Stark-themed popcorn buckets revealed for the upcoming Avengers: Endgame re-release . You can also check out our review of the VR game that released in 2020 .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).
